endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: Information should be communicated at the time that it is needed.

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Mitigation measures might include warnings to the users, system shutdown, reprocessing of the input data, the acquisition of new input data, or the use of an alternative procedure or human judgment only.

evidence.title: Randomized Controlled Comparative Effectiveness Trial of Risk Model-Guided Clinical Decision Support for Suicide Screening
evidence.outcome: Decision to screen for suicidal ideation; documented suicide risk assessments
evidence.effect: Interruptive CDS: 42% (121/289) decisions to screen vs 4% (12/307) non-interruptive (OR 17.7, p<0.001); documented assessments 63/289 vs 11/307 (p<0.001).
evidence.quote: Adjusting for provider cluster effects, Interruptive CDS led to significantly higher numbers of decisions to screen (42%=121/289 encounters) compared to Non-Interruptive CDS (4%=12/307) (odds ratio=17.7, p-value <0.001).

evidence.title: Risk Model-Guided Clinical Decision Support for Suicide Screening: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.outcome: Clinician decisions to perform in-person suicide risk screening
evidence.effect: Interruptive alerts prompted screening in 121 of 289 encounters [42%], versus 12 of 307 encounters [4%] with noninterruptive icons (odds ratio, 17.70; 95% CI, 6.42-48.79; P < .001).
evidence.quote: Accounting for cluster effects by individual clinicians, the interruptive CDS prompted higher rates of in-person screening compared with noninterruptive CDS (odds ratio, 17.70; 95% CI, 6.42-48.79; P < .001), consistent with the study alternative hypothesis.

evidence.title: Threshold and Predictive Alerts of Continuous Glucose Monitoring and Glycemic Control in Hospitalized Adults With Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.outcome: Time in target glucose range with threshold and predictive alerts enabled versus disabled
evidence.effect: Threshold alerts versus alerts off: adjusted TIR difference 3.9% [95% CI, 0.1%-7.8%]; Holm-adjusted P = .04. Adding predictive alerts: −0.8% [95% CI −4.7% to 3.0%]; Holm-adjusted P = .61.
evidence.quote: In this randomized clinical trial of hospitalized adults with diabetes, CGM threshold alerts modestly improved glycemic control compared with CGM use without alerts, whereas the addition of predictive alerts did not confer further glycemic benefit beyond threshold alerts alone.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence improves transfer times and ischemic stroke workflow metrics
evidence.venue: Interventional neuroradiology : journal of peritherapeutic neuroradiology, surgical procedures and related neurosciences
evidence.outcome: Door-to-puncture and transfer times with active smartphone AI notification
evidence.effect: Door-to-puncture time decreased 15 min (p = 0.009); transfer time from outside hospitals using Viz.ai reduced 37 min (p = 0.04); no significant change at hospitals without Viz.ai.
evidence.quote: Door-to-puncture time decreased 15 min (p = 0.009) after the implementation of Viz.ai at our Comprehensive Stroke Center.

evidence.title: Real-World Performance of Pneumothorax-Detecting Artificial Intelligence Algorithm and its Impact on Radiologist Reporting Times
evidence.outcome: Radiologist reporting time for confirmed pneumothorax with versus without PACS-integrated AI alerts
evidence.effect: Median reporting time was reduced by 46% with AI integration versus without integration (100 vs. 186 min, p < .001).
evidence.quote: Median reporting time in CXRs with radiologist-confirmed PTx was reduced by 46% in those with AI integration as compared to those without AI integration (100 vs. 186 min, p < .001).

evidence.title: Impact of Deep Learning-Based Computer-Aided Detection and Electronic Notification System for Pneumothorax on Time to Treatment: Clinical Implementation
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.outcome: Time to treatment for pneumothorax, CAD plus electronic notification vs CAD-only
evidence.effect: TTT for oxygen reduced -143.8 min (95% CI -277.8 to -9.9; P=.035); no significant difference for aspiration/tube thoracostomy (14.4 min) or thoracic surgery consultation (86.3 min).
evidence.quote: There was a significant reduction in TTT for supplemental oxygen therapy for the CAD and ENS group compared with the CAD-only group in the postimplementation period (-143.8 min; 95% confidence interval [CI], -277.8 to -9.9; P = .035).

evidence.title: Using an Artificial Intelligence Application Expedited ENRICH Trial Patient Screening: A Single Center Experience
evidence.outcome: Time from CT Head to neurosurgical-team notification for trial screening
evidence.effect: Immediate smartphone notification reduced notification time by 50 minutes (p<0.002), increasing to 57 minutes when hemorrhages not identified by the ICH algorithm were excluded.
evidence.quote: Time between CT Head and notification of the neurosurgical team for trial screening was reduced by 50 minutes after the implementation of VizAI (p<0.002).

evidence.title: Effect of Tiered Implementation of Clinical Decision Support System for Acute Kidney Injury and Nephrotoxin Exposure in Cardiac Surgery Patients
evidence.outcome: Nephrotoxin discontinuation within 30 hours after AKI across alert eras
evidence.effect: Discontinuation rose from 6 (25%) pre AKI-alert era to 14 (54%) post nephrotoxin-alert era; p = 0.047 for trend.
evidence.quote: Tiered implementation of CDSS for recognition of AKI and nephrotoxin exposure resulted in a progressive improvement in the discontinuation of nephrotoxins.

evidence.title: Incidence of cardiac arrest following implementation of a predictive analytics display in a pediatric intensive care unit
evidence.outcome: Cardiac arrest incidence and return of spontaneous circulation
evidence.effect: After display implementation, cardiac arrests decreased from 3.0 to 2.4 per 1000 patient days (non-significant); ROSC increased 50% (p = 0.025); arrests without ROSC decreased from 1.4 to 0.4 per 1000 patient days (p = 0.01).
evidence.quote: We observed a non-significant decrease in the rates of cardiac arrest events and an increase in the rate of cardiac arrests events where ROSC was achieved following the implementation of a predictive analytics display of risk scores.

evidence.title: Nephrologist's Perceptions of Risk of Severe Chronic Kidney Disease and Outpatient Follow-up After Hospitalization With AKI: Multinational Randomized Survey Study
evidence.venue: Canadian journal of kidney health and disease
evidence.outcome: Nephrologist follow-up recommendations by CKD risk
evidence.effect: Reported risk changed Likert scores: <10% mean difference = -0.71 [95% CI = -1.19, -0.23]; ≥50% mean difference = 0.49 [95% CI = 0.04, 0.93].
evidence.quote: Nephrologists were significantly less likely to recommend outpatient nephrology follow-up for patients with a <10% predicted risk of severe CKD when the risk was reported (mean difference = -0.71 [95% CI = -1.19, -0.23]), and significantly more likely to recommend follow-up for patients with a ≥50% predicted risk when the risk of severe CKD was reported (mean difference = 0.49 [95% CI = 0.04, 0.93]).

evidence.title: Implementation of Passive Deterioration Index Alerts in an Intermediate Care Unit: A Failed Early Warning System Strategy
evidence.outcome: Charge nurse documented acknowledgment of passive alerts
evidence.effect: Alert acknowledgment documented in 18.6% of cases; nurses preferred interruptive alerts and more prominent display locations.
evidence.quote: Charge nurses documented acknowledgment of the alert in 18.6% of cases, and acceptance was poor.

evidence.title: "I worry we'll blow right by it:" Barriers to Uptake of the STRATIFY-CDS for Acute Heart Failure
evidence.outcome: Ability of ED clinicians to find and launch the CDS tool within the workflow
evidence.effect: Main interface had high perceived usability, but participants struggled to find the launch button; poor launch button visibility impaired uptake (3% utilization in first 3 months).
evidence.quote: Although the main user interface had high perceived usability, participants struggled to find the launch button.

evidence.title: Appropriateness and utility of a clinical decision support system at the digital front door
evidence.outcome: Physician pre-consultation review of EHR-integrated CDSS report
evidence.effect: Only 60 of 163 surveyed consultations (37%) involved pre-consultation report review; report was accessible but not surfaced where physicians prepare for consultations.
evidence.quote: Despite the positive findings among physicians who reviewed the report, only 60 of 163 surveyed consultations (37%) involved pre-consultation report review.

commentary.bottom_line: Nine distinct studies suggest that surfacing AI outputs and alerts inside the workflow at the point of decision may increase clinician action and shorten response times, though one trial found that adding predictive alerts to threshold alerts did not improve glucose control. Certainty is low because most studies are nonrandomized, outcomes are mostly process measures, and no study compares in-interface delivery with labeling alone.

perspectives.view: Two of the ten records appear to report the same 596-encounter suicide-screening trial, so the base is nine studies. In that trial, screening rose from 4% to 42% with interruptive alerts. The glucose trial found a 3.9% gain for threshold alerts and a -0.8% difference for predictive alerts. The remaining studies are nonrandomized, which supports a low rating.

Patient-level outcomes are sparse. Arrests without return of circulation fell from 1.4 to 0.4 per 1000 patient days after a display launched, and nephrotoxin discontinuation rose from 25% to 54%. Both studies lack comparators, so secular trends may explain part of the change. Electronic notification sped oxygen for pneumothorax by 143.8 minutes but did not speed procedures.

PACS-integrated alerts cut median pneumothorax reporting time from 186 to 100 minutes, and smartphone notification shortened stroke and hemorrhage workflows by 15 to 57 minutes. Hazard studies found 18.6% acknowledgment of passive alerts, 3% use of a tool with a hard-to-find launch button, and 37% report review. These show the problem exists but do not test the fix.

No study reports enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and several do not report the country. Interface effects measured among clinicians at the sites studied may not carry over to settings with different staffing, EHR configurations, or patient mixes.

FDA draft guidance states that information should be communicated at the time it is needed, and FUTURE-AI lists user warnings among possible mitigations. Neither source specifies interruptive or passive formats. The suicide-screening trial compared formats at the same point in the workflow, which suggests that interface documentation may need to address display format as well as timing.

The studies do not report cost, alert fatigue, or clinician time spent responding to alerts. In the glucose trial, predictive alerts added no benefit beyond threshold alerts, which suggests that more alerts do not always yield more gain. Systems considering interruptive designs have no data here on the workload those designs impose.

In a vignette study of 203 nephrologists, displayed risk shifted follow-up recommendations downward for low risk and upward for high risk. This suggests that what appears on screen can change the care patients receive. No study measured patient understanding, patient trust, or patients' ability to reach a clinician about an AI-driven decision.

commentary.research_gap: No study directly compares delivering AI outputs and safety information in the interface at the point of decision with delivering them only in labeling or documentation. Trials that vary timing and format separately, measure patient outcomes alongside alert burden and override rates, and report results for underserved populations would address the main gaps.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the studies reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and several do not report the setting. The findings therefore cannot show whether in-workflow delivery works the same way, or carries the same burden, in the settings where these patients receive care.
